health_implication: Primary fatty acid in EVOO; raises HDL (good) cholesterol and reduces LDL oxidation — oxidised LDL is the form that accumulates in artery walls. Supports heart health and is thought to underlie much of EVOO's cardiovascular benefit.
source: USDA FoodData Central FDC #748608 (Olive oil, salted)

nutrient: Polyphenols (up to 500 mg/kg in high-quality Cretan EVOO)
health_implication: Anti-inflammatory and antioxidant; the polyphenol concentration is what distinguishes high-quality Cretan EVOO from commodity olive oil. Oleocanthal inhibits COX-1/COX-2 enzymes (same as ibuprofen); hydroxytyrosol is among the most potent natural antioxidants known.
source: EFSA (2011) health claim regulation (EU 432/2012) minimum 5 mg hydroxytyrosol+derivatives per 20 g EVOO; Cretan EVOO polyphenol range from study_id=1,2 in DB (Noce 2021; Esposito 2025 review)

health_implication: Fat-soluble antioxidant that protects cell membranes from oxidative damage. Works synergistically with EVOO's polyphenols. Contributes to skin health, immune function, and protection of LDL cholesterol from oxidation.
source: USDA FoodData Central FDC #748608 (Olive oil, salted)

health_implication: Essential for blood clotting cascade and for activating proteins that direct calcium into bones rather than artery walls. Regular consumption contributes meaningfully to daily vitamin K requirements.
source: USDA FoodData Central FDC #748608 (Olive oil, salted)

health_implication: Immune system function, collagen synthesis for skin and connective tissue, and iron absorption enhancer. Also a water-soluble antioxidant. A 100g serving provides over 50% of daily requirements.
source: Petropoulos et al. (2016) Food Chemistry — nutritional composition of C. spinosum; values consistent with Ntatsi et al. (2020) J Sci Food Agric

health_implication: Essential for blood clotting and bone mineralisation. Activates osteocalcin, the protein that binds calcium into bone matrix. Regular intake supports long-term bone density.
source: Petropoulos et al. (2019) Foods — phytochemical and nutritional profile of C. spinosum

health_implication: Converted to vitamin A in the body; essential for eye health (night vision), immune function, and skin integrity. A potent antioxidant in its own right — helps neutralise free radicals in tissues.
source: Petropoulos et al. (2016) Food Chemistry; Chatzigianni et al. (2019) J Sci Food Agric

health_implication: Carotenoids that accumulate specifically in the macula of the eye, where they act as a natural filter against harmful blue light and oxidative damage. Associated with reduced risk of age-related macular degeneration and cataracts.
source: Chatzigianni et al. (2019) J Sci Food Agric — carotenoid profile of Cichorium spinosum ecotypes

health_implication: Plant-derived omega-3 fatty acid; precursor to EPA and DHA. Anti-inflammatory, cardiovascular-protective, and contributes to cell membrane health. Wild-foraged stamnagathi contains more ALA than commercially grown varieties.
source: Petropoulos et al. (2016) Food Chemistry — fatty acid profile of C. spinosum

health_implication: Essential for haemoglobin synthesis and oxygen transport to cells. Iron deficiency is the world's most common nutritional deficiency; stamnagathi as a regular dietary green contributes to iron intake, particularly when consumed with vitamin C (which enhances absorption).
source: Petropoulos et al. (2016) Food Chemistry; Ntatsi et al. (2020) J Sci Food Agric

health_implication: Bone density, muscle contraction, nerve signal transmission, and blood clotting. Regular consumption of calcium-rich greens like stamnagathi supports skeletal health, particularly important in the context of a Mediterranean diet lower in dairy than northern European diets.
source: Petropoulos et al. (2016) Food Chemistry; Ntatsi et al. (2020) J Sci Food Agric

health_implication: The primary source of thyme honey's biological activity — antimicrobial (disrupts bacterial membranes), anti-inflammatory (polyphenol NF-κB suppression), and antioxidant (DPPH IC50 ~15 mg/mL). Thyme honey has among the highest total phenolic content of any honey variety.
source: George et al. (2025) Biomolecules — total phenolic content of Greek thyme honey (193 mg GAE/100g); study_id=13 in DB (Nazzaro 2024)

health_implication: Notably high for a honey; most honey varieties contain negligible vitamin C. Contributes to antioxidant capacity and immune support. Preserved only when consumed raw — heating destroys vitamin C.
source: Lafraxo et al. (2021) J Func Foods — vitamin C content measured in thyme honey fraction (study_id=12 in DB)

health_implication: Primary energy source. Higher fructose:glucose ratio than many honeys means slower crystallisation and a modestly lower glycaemic response than sucrose for the fructose component. Fructose is absorbed more slowly than glucose, blunting blood sugar spikes compared to refined sugar.
source: USDA FoodData Central FDC #169640 (Honey)

health_implication: Present in small but meaningful amounts. Manganese is a cofactor for superoxide dismutase (the body's primary antioxidant enzyme). Zinc supports immune function and wound healing. Selenium is a component of glutathione peroxidase — an antioxidant enzyme.
source: USDA FoodData Central FDC #169640 (Honey); mineral profile consistent across varietal honey literature

health_implication: Anti-inflammatory flavones that inhibit COX enzymes and reduce NF-κB pathway activation. Luteolin and apigenin are the primary compounds behind the anti-inflammatory and anxiolytic effects observed in clinical trials of mountain tea.
source: study_id=3 (Wightman 2018 DB) and study_id=4 (Papanikolaou 2024 DB); Tadić et al. (2008) Nat Prod Commun — flavonoid quantification in Sideritis syriaca

health_implication: Phenylpropanoid glycosides with exceptionally strong NF-κB binding (Kd 0.01 μM for verbascoside). The key mechanistic driver of mountain tea's anti-inflammatory activity. Also inhibits monoamine reuptake, contributing to mood and cognition effects.
source: study_id=4 in DB (Papanikolaou 2024); Kırmızıbekmez et al. (2009) Nat Prod Commun — verbascoside/acteoside in Sideritis spp.

nutrient: Iron (dried herb ~10 mg/100g dry weight; trace in infusion)
health_implication: Mountain tea as a dried herb is iron-rich; the infusion contains smaller but meaningful amounts. Regular consumption across several cups contributes to daily iron intake, particularly valued in traditional Cretan culture for combating altitude fatigue.
source: USDA FoodData Central FDC #171918 (Tea, herbal, brewed — used as proxy; dried herb value from Sideritis spp. literature)

health_implication: Electrolyte essential for blood pressure regulation, muscle contraction, and heart rhythm. Traditional consumption of mountain tea as a daily warming drink contributes meaningfully to potassium intake.
source: USDA FoodData Central FDC #171918 (Tea, herbal, brewed — used as proxy; dried herb value from Sideritis spp. literature)

health_implication: Graviera is one of the highest-calcium foods available — a 30g serving provides ~210-240 mg calcium, approximately 20-25% of daily requirements. Calcium is essential for bone density (preventing osteoporosis), muscle contraction, nerve transmission, and blood clotting. The vitamin K2 in Graviera works synergistically to direct this calcium into bones rather than arteries.
source: USDA FoodData Central FDC #172179 (Gruyere cheese); extrapolated to Graviera as comparable aged sheep/goat hard cheese. Graviera PDO composition data from EFET (Greek Food Authority)

health_implication: Complete protein containing all essential amino acids. Supports muscle maintenance and repair, immune antibody synthesis, enzyme production, and provides satiety. Particularly valuable for older adults where muscle mass preservation is critical.
source: USDA FoodData Central FDC #172179 (Gruyere cheese); extrapolated to Graviera as comparable aged sheep/goat hard cheese

health_implication: Essential for neurological function, red blood cell formation, and DNA synthesis. Deficiency causes irreversible nerve damage. Animal dairy is one of the few reliable dietary sources; a 50g serving of Graviera provides ~75% of daily B12 requirements.
source: USDA FoodData Central FDC #172179 (Gruyere cheese); extrapolated to Graviera as comparable aged sheep/goat hard cheese

health_implication: Produced by bacteria during cheese aging; activates matrix Gla-protein (MGP) which prevents calcium from depositing in artery walls — this mechanism may explain why cheese consumption is inversely associated with cardiovascular disease despite its saturated fat content (the calcium paradox). Directs calcium into bones where it belongs.
source: Schurgers & Vermeer (2000) Haemostasis — MK-8 and MK-9 content of fermented cheeses; study_id=8,10 in DB (Zhang 2023 umbrella review; Zoumpopoulou 2018)

health_implication: Works with calcium in bone and teeth mineralisation — approximately 85% of the body's phosphorus is in bones and teeth. Also essential for ATP (cellular energy currency) synthesis and cell membrane structure.
source: USDA FoodData Central FDC #172179 (Gruyere cheese); extrapolated to Graviera as comparable aged sheep/goat hard cheese

health_implication: Supports immune function, wound healing, protein synthesis, taste and smell perception, and DNA repair. A 50g serving of Graviera provides ~15% of daily zinc requirements.
source: USDA FoodData Central FDC #172179 (Gruyere cheese); extrapolated to Graviera as comparable aged sheep/goat hard cheese

nutrient: Conjugated linoleic acid / CLA (higher in grass-fed Cretan sheep dairy)
health_implication: Natural trans-fat produced in the rumen of grass-fed ruminants; absent or low in grain-fed dairy. Anti-inflammatory, may reduce body fat accumulation and support immune function. Cretan sheep and goat raised on aromatic mountain pasture produce milk with notably higher CLA than conventionally farmed animals.
source: Nudda et al. (2003) J Dairy Sci — CLA content of sheep milk and cheese; Tsiplakou et al. (2006) J Dairy Res — CLA in Greek sheep/goat milk by feeding system; extrapolated to Graviera

health_implication: Purslane is the richest known leafy vegetable source of ALA — far exceeding spinach or kale. ALA is converted to EPA and DHA (marine omega-3s) in the body; reduces cardiovascular disease risk, lowers triglycerides, reduces systemic inflammation, and supports cell membrane fluidity. The omega-3 content partly explains the traditional Cretan diet's cardiovascular protection even without high fish consumption.
source: Simopoulos & Salem (1986) NEJM — original identification of purslane as richest plant ALA source; USDA FoodData Central FDC #169226; study_id=6 in DB (Guo 2024 meta-analysis)

health_implication: Immune function, collagen synthesis for skin and connective tissue, antioxidant activity, and enhancement of iron absorption from plant sources. A 100g serving provides ~23% of daily vitamin C requirements.
source: USDA FoodData Central FDC #169226 (Purslane, raw)

health_implication: Converted to vitamin A — essential for eye health, immune function, skin integrity, and gene expression. Works as a fat-soluble antioxidant. Absorption is enhanced when eaten with olive oil, as in traditional Cretan salads.
source: USDA FoodData Central FDC #169226 (Purslane, raw)

health_implication: Fat-soluble antioxidant protecting cell membranes from oxidative damage. Works with vitamin C and other antioxidants in a synergistic network. Particularly important for protecting the omega-3 fatty acids in purslane from oxidation.
source: USDA FoodData Central FDC #169226 (Purslane, raw)

health_implication: Essential for over 300 enzyme reactions; supports muscle and nerve function, blood pressure regulation, blood glucose control, and protein synthesis. A 100g serving provides ~17% of daily requirements. Magnesium deficiency is common in Western diets.
source: USDA FoodData Central FDC #169226 (Purslane, raw)

health_implication: Regulates blood pressure by counterbalancing sodium; supports heart rhythm, muscle contraction, and fluid balance. A 100g serving provides ~10% of daily requirements. High-potassium diets are consistently associated with lower cardiovascular disease risk.
source: USDA FoodData Central FDC #169226 (Purslane, raw)

health_implication: Contributes to haemoglobin synthesis and oxygen transport. Plant-source (non-haem) iron absorption is enhanced by the vitamin C in purslane and by eating with acidic dressings (lemon juice). The combination of iron + vitamin C in purslane makes it a self-enhancing source of this nutrient.
source: USDA FoodData Central FDC #169226 (Purslane, raw)

nutrient: Melatonin (notably high for a plant food)
health_implication: Purslane is one of the highest plant sources of melatonin. Beyond its role in regulating circadian rhythms and sleep quality, melatonin acts as a potent antioxidant and anti-inflammatory compound in peripheral tissues. May contribute to purslane's anti-inflammatory profile alongside ALA and polyphenols.
source: Tan et al. (2012) J Exp Bot — melatonin content across plant foods; purslane identified as exceptional source among leafy vegetables

nutrient: Essential oils (carvacrol ~52% of EO; gamma-terpinene; p-cymene)
health_implication: Primary bioactive fraction of dittany; carvacrol responsible for strong antimicrobial activity against Gram-positive and Gram-negative pathogens; also antioxidant and enzyme-inhibitory. Concentration in herbal infusion is lower than essential oil but retains pharmacological relevance at traditional consumption levels.

nutrient: Polyphenols (rosmarinic acid; apigenin; kaempferol; quercetin; novel luteolin glycosides)
health_implication: Complex polyphenol profile including novel flavone glycosides unique to dittany; contributes antioxidant capacity, anti-inflammatory activity (NF-kB inhibition), and spasmolytic gut effects. Rosmarinic acid is the dominant polar phenolic.
source: Chatzopoulou et al. (2010) DOI 10.1021/jf904596m; Paloukopoulou et al. (2026) DOI 10.1016/j.foodchem.2026.148243
